lead: A thick cylinder is one whose wall is not small compared with its radius, roughly diameter-to-thickness below 20. The thin-cylinder formula assumes hoop stress is constant through the wall; Lame's theory accepts that it is not. It writes radial stress σ<sub>r</sub> = A − B/r² and hoop stress σ<sub>θ</sub> = A + B/r², with constants A and B fixed by the pressures at the bore and outside. The result is used for hydraulic cylinders, gun barrels, pressure vessels, pipe autofrettage and high-pressure process equipment, where, under internal pressure, the bore is normally the danger point and the first point to yield.
prereq: You need: 7.5 for the thin-wall force balance, and see Unit 2 for principal stresses and maximum shear.

blocks.text: Thin-cylinder theory balances force on a cut half-cylinder, then divides by the wall area. It gives σ<sub>θ</sub> = p d/(2t), where p is internal pressure, d is internal diameter and t is wall thickness. That formula returns one number, so it assumes hoop stress is uniform through the wall. The assumption is fair while the wall is thin: d/t above about 20. Below d/t ≈ 20, material near the bore stretches more than material outside and shares the load differently. The hoop stress then varies strongly across the wall. Hydraulic press cylinders, gun barrels and high-pressure process pipes with thick walls fall in this group. The thin formula can be badly low at the bore, so it is unsafe there. Lame's theory keeps the force balance but lets stress change with radius r.

Take a ring of unit length along the axis, between radius r and r + dr. Radial stress σ<sub>r</sub> acts on the inner and outer curved faces. Hoop stress σ<sub>θ</sub> acts on the two side faces. Radial equilibrium of the ring gives dσ<sub>r</sub>/dr + (σ<sub>r</sub> − σ<sub>θ</sub>)/r = 0. Strain compatibility with Hooke's law adds that σ<sub>r</sub> + σ<sub>θ</sub> is constant. Solving these conditions gives Lame's equations:
σ<sub>r</sub> = A − B/r²,   σ<sub>θ</sub> = A + B/r²
blocks.where: σ<sub>r</sub> is radial stress (negative in compression), σ<sub>θ</sub> is hoop stress, r is radius in m, A is in MPa, B is in MPa m² so that B/r² is in MPa.

blocks.text: A and B are constants fixed by the pressures at the two surfaces. Boundary conditions for internal pressure p only: at the bore r = r<sub>i</sub>, σ<sub>r</sub> = −p; at the outer surface r = r<sub>o</sub>, σ<sub>r</sub> = 0. Solving gives:
A = p r<sub>i</sub>²/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²),   B = p r<sub>i</sub>² r<sub>o</sub>²/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²)
blocks.where: p is internal pressure in MPa, r<sub>i</sub> is bore radius in m, r<sub>o</sub> is outer radius in m.

blocks.text: σ<sub>θ,bore</sub> = p(r<sub>o</sub>² + r<sub>i</sub>²)/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²),   σ<sub>θ,outer</sub> = 2p r<sub>i</sub>²/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²)
blocks.where: σ<sub>θ,bore</sub> is hoop stress at the inside surface, σ<sub>θ,outer</sub> is hoop stress at the outside surface.

blocks.text: At the bore σ<sub>θ</sub> is largest. At the outer surface it is lower. For closed ends, the end pressure is carried by longitudinal stress σ<sub>L</sub> = p r<sub>i</sub>²/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²) = A.

At the bore, σ<sub>θ</sub> is largest and σ<sub>r</sub> is −p, so the difference is largest there. For a closed cylinder the three principal stresses at the bore are σ<sub>θ</sub>, σ<sub>L</sub> and σ<sub>r</sub>. The largest shear stress is τ<sub>max</sub> = (σ<sub>θ</sub> − σ<sub>r</sub>)/2 = (σ<sub>θ,bore</sub> + p)/2. The outer surface has lower hoop stress and zero radial stress, so it is not the danger point. Design checks therefore use the bore: yield begins there first. In the worked example, the bore has 100 MPa hoop and −60 MPa radial, giving τ<sub>max</sub> = 80 MPa; the thin formula would have said 60 MPa everywhere. Some books call this Lame's theory, some the thick-cylinder theory. Use the same sign convention throughout: tensile positive, radial compression at the bore negative.

figure.caption: At the bore the hoop stress is 100 MPa and the radial stress is −60 MPa; at the outer surface they are 40 MPa and 0. Notice that the average of the two stresses is always A = 20 MPa, the longitudinal stress for closed ends.

spec.aria: Across the wall of a thick cylinder, hoop stress falls from 100 MPa at the bore to 40 MPa outside while radial stress rises from minus 60 MPa to zero.

examples.question: A thick cylinder has internal radius 50 mm, external radius 100 mm and carries internal pressure 60 MPa, with no external pressure. Find the constants A and B, the hoop stress at the bore and at the outer surface, the longitudinal stress for closed ends, and the maximum shear stress at the bore.
steps: Convert radii to metres: r<sub>i</sub> = 50 mm = 0.05 m, r<sub>o</sub> = 100 mm = 0.1 m. The pressure is p = 60 MPa.
Use σ<sub>r</sub> = A − B/r². At the bore: A − B/0.05² = −60. At the outer surface: A − B/0.1² = 0.
The outer condition gives A = B/r<sub>o</sub>² = B/0.1² = B/0.01 = 100B.
Substitute in the bore condition: 100B − B/0.0025 = −60, so 100B − 400B = −60, giving −300B = −60 and B = 0.2 MPa m².
Hoop stress at the bore: σ<sub>θ,bore</sub> = A + B/r<sub>i</sub>² = 20 + 0.2/0.0025 = 20 + 80 = 100 MPa.
Hoop stress at the outer surface: σ<sub>θ,outer</sub> = A + B/r<sub>o</sub>² = 20 + 0.2/0.01 = 20 + 20 = 40 MPa.
Longitudinal stress for closed ends: σ<sub>L</sub> = p r<sub>i</sub>²/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²) = 60 × 0.0025/0.0075 = 20 MPa, which equals A.
Maximum shear at the bore: τ<sub>max</sub> = (σ<sub>θ,bore</sub> − σ<sub>r,bore</sub>)/2 = (100 − (−60))/2 = 80 MPa.
examples.answer: The constants are A = 20 MPa and B = 0.2 MPa m², the hoop stress is 100 MPa at the bore and 40 MPa at the outer surface, the longitudinal stress is 20 MPa, and the maximum shear at the bore is 80 MPa.
examples.check:
ri = 0.05
ro = 0.10
p = 60.0
den = ro**2 - ri**2
A = p * ri**2 / den
B = p * ri**2 * ro**2 / den
hoop_bore = A + B / ri**2
hoop_outer = A + B / ro**2
sigma_L = p * ri**2 / den
tau_bore = (hoop_bore - (-p)) / 2.0
print(A)
print(B)
print(hoop_bore)
print(hoop_outer)
print(sigma_L)
print(tau_bore)

traps: Writing σ<sub>r</sub> = +p at the bore. Internal pressure pushes on the bore, so radial stress is compression: σ<sub>r</sub> = −p at r = r<sub>i</sub>.
Using millimetres in B/r². B is in MPa m², so r must be in metres; 50 mm must become 0.05 m.
Applying σ<sub>θ</sub> = p d/(2t) when d/t is below 20. The thin formula gives 60 MPa for the worked example, not the true 100 MPa at the bore.
Checking the outer surface for maximum shear. σ<sub>θ</sub> and the difference σ<sub>θ</sub> − σ<sub>r</sub> are largest at the bore, so the bore is the danger point.
Forgetting the closed-end longitudinal stress. It is p r<sub>i</sub>²/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²), equal to A here, and it makes the stress state triaxial at the bore.

quiz.q: Write Lame's equations for a thick cylinder and state the units of A and B.
quiz.a: σ<sub>r</sub> = A − B/r² and σ<sub>θ</sub> = A + B/r², with A in MPa, B in MPa m² and r in m.

quiz.q: Why is hoop stress not uniform in a thick cylinder?
quiz.a: Material near the bore stretches more than material outside. Radial equilibrium and strain compatibility then force the hoop stress to vary with radius; the thin theory wrongly assumes one uniform value.

quiz.q: For p = 60 MPa, r<sub>i</sub> = 50 mm and r<sub>o</sub> = 100 mm, find the hoop stress at the bore.
quiz.a: A = 20 MPa and B = 0.2 MPa m². σ<sub>θ,bore</sub> = A + B/r<sub>i</sub>² = 20 + 0.2/0.05² = 100 MPa.

quiz.q: Where is the maximum shear stress in a thick cylinder under internal pressure, and why?
quiz.a: At the bore. The hoop stress is largest there and the radial stress is −p, so τ<sub>max</sub> = (σ<sub>θ</sub> − σ<sub>r</sub>)/2 is largest; in the worked example it is (100 − (−60))/2 = 80 MPa.

quiz.q: For the same cylinder, find the longitudinal stress for closed ends.
quiz.a: σ<sub>L</sub> = p r<sub>i</sub>²/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²) = 60 × 0.0025/0.0075 = 20 MPa, which is equal to A.

quiz.q: State the two boundary conditions used for a thick cylinder with internal pressure p only.
quiz.a: At the bore r = r<sub>i</sub>, σ<sub>r</sub> = −p. At the outer surface r = r<sub>o</sub>, σ<sub>r</sub> = 0.

quiz.q: Compare the thin formula with Lame's theory at the bore and at the outer surface for the worked example.
quiz.a: The thin formula gives 60 MPa everywhere. Lame's theory gives 100 MPa at the bore and 40 MPa at the outer surface. The thin formula is unsafe at the bore and wrong about the distribution through the wall.

beyond: Not for the exam. Autofrettage uses this stress distribution: the bore is yielded on purpose, so on release it carries a compressive residual hoop stress that delays fatigue cracking. The same equations feed burst-pressure calculations, shrink-fit design and finite-element checks of pressure vessels. Search for Lame's thick cylinder, autofrettage, and ASME pressure vessel code if you want the design side.
